This walks through one analysis end to end: connecting, finding out what the
variables mean, fetching the data, joining two waves, and recording what a
published figure was computed from.

Nothing here runs when the vignette is built — the code needs a platform and a
token of your own.

## Connecting

Create a token under **your account menu → API Tokens** on your platform, then
put it in your environment rather than in the script:

```
# ~/.Renviron
SONDAVI_TOKEN=sdv_…
```

Restart R, and:

```{r}
library(sondavi)

con <- sondavi_connect("https://survey.your-institute.org")
```

A token written into an analysis script travels with it into version control,
onto shared drives and into supplementary material. That is the most common way
one leaks, which is why `sondavi_connect()` reads the environment by default.

## What is there

```{r}
sondavi_surveys(con)
#>    id                  title project    status       privacy response_count
#> 1  42       Wave 1 baseline   Ageing published     identified            318
#> 2  43       Wave 2 follow-up  Ageing published     identified            274
```

The token only ever shows the studies it was given. If one is missing, the token
was scoped to something narrower — that is the scope, not an error.

## What the variables mean

```{r}
cb <- sondavi_codebook(con, 42)
cb[, c("name", "label", "type")]
#>                  name                        label        type
#> 1                 age             How old are you?      string
#> 2                mood            How is your mood? categorical
#> 3 ratings.speed.score Rate the study — Speed × score     numeric
```

This is the part a CSV cannot carry: the intended type and the value labels
behind each code.

```{r}
cb$value_labels[[2]]
#>   value    text
#> 1     1     Bad
#> 2     2 Neutral
#> 3     3    Good
```

## The data

```{r}
d <- sondavi_responses(con, 42)
```

All pages are fetched for you, and the codebook is applied: `mood` arrives as a
factor with those labels rather than as `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, and every column
carries its question text.

```{r}
table(d$mood)
attr(d$mood, "label")
#> [1] "How is your mood?"
```

### Two things worth knowing before you count anything

**Partial responses are included** when the study saves them, exactly as in the
platform's export. Someone who stopped halfway is a row whose `completed_at` is
`NA` - and so is someone the study screened out, whose row carries `screened_out_at`
and `screen_out_reason` instead:

```{r}
nrow(d)                                           # everyone who started
table(d$response_status)                          # complete, partial, screened_out
done <- subset(d, response_status == "complete")  # everyone who finished
```

**Timestamps are timestamps**, not text, so durations work directly:

```{r}
summary(as.numeric(difftime(done$completed_at, done$started_at, units = "mins")))
```

### Nested questions

Matrices and dynamic panels arrive as list columns — flattening them on arrival
would invent a shape the platform did not give. When you want the flat form:

```{r}
flat <- sondavi_unnest(d)
names(flat)
#> … "ratings.speed.score" "ratings.clarity.score"
```

Those are the same names the platform's own export writes, so an analysis built
on an exported file and one built on the API agree on what a variable is called.
The new columns get the codebook as well: a matrix cell with value labels is a
factor, like the questions beside it.

### Questions with several answers

A multiple-choice answer is the list of options chosen - `c("phone", "other")` -
and stays one list column. `sondavi_unnest()` adds one column per option right
after it, as the export files have them: 1 when the option was chosen, 0 when
the question was answered without it, `NA` when it was not answered. For a
ranking the column holds the option's place.

```{r}
flat[, c("devices.phone", "devices.laptop", "devices.none", "devices.other")]
#>   devices.phone devices.laptop devices.none devices.other
#> 1             1              0            0             1
#> 2             0              0            1             0
#> 3            NA             NA           NA            NA
```

`sondavi_options()` does the same for data you have not unnested.

### Reverse-scored items

A scale often has an item worded the other way round ("I worry a lot" among
items about calm). Marked as "Reverse-scored" in the editor, its answer is still
stored as given, and `sondavi_unnest()` adds the reversed copy right after it -
the same column the platform's export file has:

```{r}
flat[, c("b5.worry", "b5.worry_r")]
#>   b5.worry   b5.worry_r
#> 1 A little            4
#> 2 Don't know         NA
```

`b5.worry_r` is (smallest + largest scale value) - answer, here 6 - answer on a
1-5 scale, computed from the answer as given. "Don't know" is not on the scale
and has no reversed value. The range comes from the codebook:

```{r}
cb[cb$reverse_scored, c("name", "reverse_min", "reverse_max")]
```

### Scale scores

For arithmetic the items need their numbers, not their labels. `as.numeric()` on
a factor gives the position of the level - "Don't know", the sixth option, would
become 6. `sondavi_scale()` takes the numbers from the codebook and uses the
reversed copy for a reverse-scored item, so the items are named as in the
questionnaire:

```{r}
flat$b5_score <- sondavi_scale(flat, c("b5.calm", "b5.worry"))
sondavi_items(flat, c("b5.calm", "b5.worry"))    # the numbers behind it
#>   b5.calm b5.worry_r
#> 1       4          4
#> 2       6         NA
```

The score is `NA` unless every item has a number; `min_items` allows gaps on
purpose, `method = "sum"` adds instead of averaging. `sondavi_items()` is what
`cor()` or `psych::alpha()` want.

A score the questionnaire computes itself (Σ in the editor, with subscales if
the rows have them) is stored with every response, as it was computed then. To
work it out again - for responses recorded before you added or changed it -
name it; the codebook says which rows it counts, mean or sum and how many have
to be answered:

```{r}
flat$sdq_emo_now <- sondavi_scale(flat, score = "sdq_emo")
cb[!is.na(cb$subscale), c("name", "subscale")]   # which row belongs to which subscale
```

### Image marking

An image marking question stores the image, the grid and the painted cells or
the pins. For a heatmap, one row per cell or pin:

```{r}
m <- sondavi_markings(d)
head(m[, c("question", "category", "row", "col", "x_px", "y_px")])
```

`x_norm`/`y_norm` are the position between 0 and 1, `x_px`/`y_px` the same in
pixels of the original image - the mapping, already done. The table is the one
the platform's image-markings export writes.

### AI interviews

An AI interview question stores the whole conversation. `sondavi_unnest()`
makes the export's columns of it (how it ended, how many answers, the chosen
summary); the conversation itself is a table of its own, one row per message:

```{r}
talk <- sondavi_conversations(d)
said <- subset(talk, role == "respondent")
aggregate(nchar(text) ~ response_id, data = said, FUN = sum)   # characters a person wrote
```

Call it before `sondavi_unnest()`, which replaces the conversation by those
columns.

## Joining waves

```{r}
d <- sondavi_waves(con, c(42, 43), names = c("baseline", "followup"))
```

Each wave's columns are suffixed, so `mood` becomes `mood_baseline` and
`mood_followup` instead of colliding. **Everyone seen in any wave is kept**: a
person who did not take the follow-up is still a row, with `NA` in its columns.

That is deliberate. Attrition is usually what a longitudinal design is about, and
an inner join would silently drop exactly the people you want to describe:

```{r}
table(returned = !is.na(d$mood_followup))
```

The match needs an identifier, so the token must carry the respondent ability and
the studies must not be anonymous. An anonymous study is not linkable by design,
and the function says so rather than guessing.

## Making the result citable

A live query is not a dataset. Run the same script next month and it may return
more rows, or fewer — new responses arrive, and retention or a data-subject
request may remove some.

The cheap version is to record the fingerprint next to your result:

```{r}
sondavi_fingerprint(d)
#> survey 42, 318 rows, fetched 2026-09-23T09:32:29+00:00, digest 332f3d2a1fbfd880
```

The better version, for anything you publish, is a snapshot:

```{r}
snap <- sondavi_snapshot(con, 42, label = "Paper, figure 2")
snap$id
#> [1] "8869174a-a6c7-4cbc-9a9e-2785dcecba51"
```

Put that UUID in the paper. A snapshot records *which* responses the figure was
computed from — never a copy of them, so erasure requests and retention keep
working on the real data.

Later, to reproduce:

```{r}
d <- sondavi_snapshot_responses(con, snap$id)
attr(d, "sondavi_complete")
#> [1] TRUE
```

If responses have been deleted since, you get a warning naming how many, and
`sondavi_complete` is `FALSE`. That is not an error — it is the answer you need
before re-running the analysis behind a published figure.

A colleague can replay your snapshot to reproduce your analysis. They never see
more than their own token allows: if yours carried identifiers and theirs does
not, they get the same rows with fewer columns, and are told that the recorded
fingerprint does not describe what they received.

## Passing on a certified dataset

If you share your data as a certified dataset from the platform — the CSV file with its
`.certificate.json` — anyone can check that every certified cell is what the participants
entered, without an account:

```{r}
v <- sondavi_verify("wave2.csv", "wave2.certificate.json")
v$valid
#> [1] TRUE
```

The keys of `https://sondavi.io` known when this version of the package was released are
built in, so such a check needs a connection only for a newer key. To pass on a version with
fewer columns or rows — without the pseudonyms, or without people who did not agree to
sharing — or in another format, certify the changed file on the platform that issued the
certificate ("Certify a file you have", compared with the certified file); that works even
after the responses were deleted there. Deleting columns or rows by hand, or saving the file
again from a spreadsheet program, makes the certificate fail.

## Fetching only what is new

For a study still collecting, ask for the increment rather than everything:

```{r}
recent <- sondavi_responses(con, 42, since = Sys.Date() - 7)
```

## When something goes wrong

The platform limits how often a token may be used and says how long to wait. The
package waits that long and retries; it does not hammer. This is the main reason
to use it rather than write the calls yourself — that, and every read being
recorded in the study's activity log under a recognisable user agent.
